guides.title: Heat mat
items: Heat mat is for GERMINATION ONLY, not for growing on.

All the front-yard heat-lovers flagged heatMat=true belong on it at seeding: bottlegourd, ridgegourd, bitter gourd, cucumber, eggplant, okra, peppers, tomatillo, roselle, basil, marigold, plus backyard kohlrabi/cabbage/cauliflower if you start those indoors.

Target 75-90F at the soil surface (use the mat's probe or a soil thermometer): okra and the gourds (lauki/turai/karela) want it warmest (85-90F), peppers/eggplant 80-85F, cucumber and basil 75-85F, brassicas 70-75F.
The instant 50-75% of a tray has emerged, take that tray OFF the mat and put it under bright light at cooler room temp - leaving sprouted seedlings on heat makes them leggy.
Bitter gourd, okra, and the gourds also need their hard seed coats soaked 24h (and nicked for karela/lauki) before they go on the mat.
For summer sowing, use the heat mat for cabbage/cauliflower starts in late June-July for the fall crop, or for a late basil tray.
Amaranth can be direct-sown into warm June soil; its optional May indoor starts benefit from 75-80F soil, with a heat mat only if the room is cool.

guides.title: Seed starting
items: Back-count from the ~Apr 15 last frost using each crop's lead time, then add ~2 weeks because Sammamish soil is not reliably >60F until late May/June - so transplant dates for heat-lovers are really late-May/early-June, not mid-April.

Typical indoor sow dates (count weeks BEFORE the late-May/June transplant): peppers, eggplant, okra, bitter gourd 8-10 wks (sow late Feb-early Mar - the slow germinators); tomatillo, roselle 6-8 wks; bottlegourd, ridgegourd, cucumber, basil 3-4 wks (cucurbits resent root disturbance - use peat/paper pots and sow early-to-mid May, NOT February).
Workflow: sow in cells, on the heat mat at the target temp above, under bright light (shop LED) once up, pot up before rootbound, and fertilize lightly once true leaves appear.

HARDENING OFF is mandatory and skipped at your peril here: 7-10 days before transplant, set plants outside 1-2 hrs in shade and increase exposure/sun/wind daily; never transplant heat-lovers until both nights are reliably above ~50F AND soil is >60F.

Direct-sow crops (sunflower, beans, peas, carrots, beets, radish, spinach, arugula, cilantro, dill, scallion) skip all this - cilantro and dill MUST be direct-sown because their taproots resent transplanting.
Brassicas (cabbage, cauliflower) start indoors 5-6 wks before transplant, and in 8b the FALL crop (sow indoors late June-July, transplant Aug) is more reliable than spring.

Amaranth is a warm-season leafy green: optionally start indoors in early-mid May, harden off for June planting, or direct sow June-late July once soil is at least 65F (ideally near 70F); sow only 1/8-1/4 in deep.

guides.title: Slugs
items: Maritime Sammamish is prime slug country, worst in the wet shaded backyard and on any soft seedling.
Highest-risk crops: cucumber/basil/marigold/sunflower seedlings in front; lettuce, spinach, cilantro, dill, cabbage, pole-bean seedlings, and all young brassicas in the shaded backyard.
Strategy: (1) Set out iron-phosphate bait (Sluggo/Sluggo Plus) - safe around pets/wildlife - the moment any direct-sown or transplanted seedling goes in, and re-bait after rain.
(2) Hand-pick at night with a flashlight during the first 2-3 weeks after sowing, which is when slugs do the real damage.
(3) Use copper tape rings on individual cloches for the most vulnerable backyard greens.
(4) Keep drip emitters from over-wetting the soil surface and clear mulch/debris a few inches back from seedling stems to remove daytime hiding spots.
(5) Start slug-prone crops as transplants where allowed (lettuce, basil, marigold) so they skip the most vulnerable seedling stage in open ground.

guides.title: Companions & pests
items: Basil and marigold are your interplanting workhorses in the full-sun front yard: tuck basil among peppers, eggplant, and tomatillo (shared heat needs, basil may deter some pests and uses the space), and ring the gourd arches and nightshades with marigold to help suppress root-knot nematodes and pull in pollinators/beneficials - important here given low bee activity.
Deadhead marigolds and pinch basil to keep both productive.

Pest groups and organic controls: (1) Brassicas (cabbage, cauliflower, kohlrabi) = cabbage worm/looper magnets - cover with floating row cover/insect netting from transplant day and spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) if caterpillars appear.
(2) Flea beetles hit arugula, radish, and eggplant - same row cover, plus the cover doubles for carrot rust fly on carrots and root maggot on radish.
(3) Cucumber beetles on cucumber and aphids on indoor pepper starts - inspect early, blast aphids with water or insecticidal soap, hand-pick beetles.
(4) Leaf miner on spinach/beet greens - remove and destroy mined leaves, use row cover.
(5) Slugs everywhere (see slug plan).
Net sunflower heads as seeds mature to beat the birds, and net pea/bean seedlings from birds too.
Dill left to flower is a deliberate beneficial-insect attractor - let some bolt at season's end to feed predators of aphids and worms.

guides.title: Trellis & arch
items: Front yard, two arch tunnels: dedicate the strongest, tallest arch to bitter gourd and bottlegourd (lauki sprawls 15 ft and lauki/karela want to hang fruit down through the arch where it grows straight) and the second arch to ridgegourd plus cucumber.
Build/anchor arches as sturdy cattle-panel or heavy-gauge welded-wire hoops on driven T-posts or rebar - a heavy gourd vine in an August wind will flatten anything flimsy.
Train vines up with soft ties for the first few feet, then let tendrils take over; use slings (old t-shirt/netting cradles) to support heavy lauki fruit so the vine does not tear.
Tomatillo is NOT a climber - cage it (it sprawls and needs support, and remember you must grow at least 2 plants for pollination/fruit set).

Backyard trellises: give sugar-snap peas a 4-6 ft net/pea-netting trellis on the north side of the planting area so they do not shade everything, and pole beans a tall 6-8 ft trellis or teepee - both fix nothing if they flop.
Orient all trellises/arches N-S or put tall structures on the north edge so they do not cast shade onto shorter front-yard heat-lovers that can least afford lost sun.

guides.title: Watering by month
items: Both yards are on drip - tune by zone and month.
FRONT (full sun, heat-lovers): cucumbers and gourds demand EVEN moisture (uneven water = bitter cukes and dropped/aborted gourd fruit), eggplant/pepper drop blossoms if stressed.
Apr-May: light, ~1x/week as soil warms and rain still falls.
June: ~2x/week, 30-45 min, deeper as plants size up.

Jul-Aug (the dry stretch, no rain): the critical period - 3-4x/week or daily short cycles for cucurbits, aiming for ~1.5 in/week total, early-morning runs; mulch heavily (black plastic for the heat-lovers doubles as moisture retention).
Sep: taper to 2x/week as nights cool and rain returns.
Oct: off, rely on rain.
BACKYARD (partial shade, cool-season): needs noticeably LESS than the front - shade plus cooler soil holds moisture.
But carrots and beets need constant surface moisture to germinate and even moisture to avoid woody/forked roots, and cabbage/cauliflower/kohlrabi split or button without steady water.
Apr-June: 1-2x/week.
Jul-Aug: 2-3x/week, watch the shallow-rooted greens.
Sep-Oct: 1x/week then off.
Run drip in early morning everywhere to cut slug-friendly overnight surface wetness and downy/powdery mildew on basil and peas.

guides.title: Crop rotation
items: Track crop families across years in both yards to avoid soilborne disease and pest buildup, and to balance heavy feeders.
FRONT YARD (full sun) families: Cucurbits (lauki, turai, karela, cucumber), Nightshades (eggplant, pepper, tomatillo), Alliums (garlic, shallots), plus basil, marigold, roselle, and sunflower.

BACKYARD families: Brassicas (cabbage, cauliflower, kohlrabi, arugula, radish), Greens (spinach, beet, chard, sorrel), Umbellifers (carrot, cilantro, dill), Legumes (peas, pole beans), Alliums (scallion), and Asteraceae (lettuce).
Move each family to a different planting spot each year, aiming for at least 3 years before returning it to the same soil.
Follow heavy-feeding brassicas with peas or beans, then light-feeding roots.
In the front yard, alternate cucurbits and nightshades between planting spots; move marigold with them as a companion.
Use roselle, sunflower, and basil as rotation buffers.
Amend heavy feeders with compost each spring.
Amaranth in the front yard is in the spinach/beet family (Amaranthaceae), so include that family when rotating its sunny patch.

guides.title: Top Tips
items: Use the maritime calendar honestly: your real heat-lover transplant window is late-May through mid-June, not the textbook 'after last frost' April date - cold soil stalls peppers/eggplant/gourds even when frost has passed.

Create a warm microclimate for the marginal heat-lovers (okra, karela, ridgegourd, eggplant, peppers): plant against a south/west-facing wall or fence, use black plastic mulch, and deploy wall-o-waters early.
This banked heat is the single biggest yield lever in cool Sammamish summers.
Plan now for the fall garden - in 8b the late-July/August sowing of brassicas, spinach, arugula, cilantro, lettuce, scallions, and overwintering crops is often MORE productive than spring.
Reserve space in the backyard for it.
Overwinter what you can: spinach, scallions, and sorrel overwinter in 8b; lettuce is frost-tolerant to ~25F; sow a fall batch and harvest into winter under simple cloches.
Hand-pollinate every gourd and the cucumber if bee activity is low - transfer pollen from male to female flowers (the one with the tiny fruit behind it) with a small brush.
Lauki opens at night, so pollinate it in the evening or very early morning.
Succession-sow the fast crops every 2-3 weeks - radish, arugula, cilantro, lettuce, and sunflowers - rather than one big planting, to spread harvest and dodge simultaneous bolting.
Row cover is a multi-tool here: same floating cover defeats cabbage worms on brassicas, flea beetles on arugula/radish/eggplant, carrot rust fly on carrots, and root maggot on radish.
Buy a roll and reuse it across the garden (remove from insect-pollinated crops at flowering).

Pinch and deadhead religiously: pinch basil and sorrel flower stalks to delay bolting, deadhead marigolds and succession sunflowers for continuous bloom, and pinch gourd growing tips once they reach the arch top to push side branching and female flowers.
Net it or lose it: birds eat pea and bean seedlings and raid maturing sunflower heads - use netting or paper bags on sunflower heads as seeds fill.

Watch downy/powdery mildew in the damp PNW - space basil and peas for airflow, water at the soil in the morning via drip (never overhead), and remove affected leaves promptly; it shows up reliably on basil in late summer and peas late-season.

guides.title: Woodland Shade
items: Part shade · acidic soil
Morning sun / afternoon shade, acidic organic soil, even moisture, mulched.
North or east side of the house, or under tree canopy.
Evergreen camellia & rhododendron anchor it; hydrangea in the middle; hosta at the shady edge.

guides.title: Sunny Cottage Border
items: Full sun · rich, well-drained
Full sun 6+ hrs with good airflow (PNW disease pressure).
Hollyhock at the back (tall), roses + peony in the middle, shasta daisy at the front.
Stake peony & hollyhock.

guides.title: Spring Bulbs
items: Full sun · sharp drainage
Plant in fall (Oct–Nov), bloom Mar–May.
Tuck into the cottage border or pots.
Hyacinth perennializes here; tulips are often short-lived in our wet summers.

guides.title: Edible & Foliage Accents
items: Full sun
Blueberry wants the same acidic soil as the rhodies but needs sun — plant 2+ varieties for cross-pollination.
Barberry is a tough, thorny, colorful, low-care hedge/accent.
